pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 10–11 years

- **Topic:** The Circulatory System

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y6 'Animals, including humans'):** "identify and name the main parts of the human circulatory system, and describe the functions of the heart, blood vessels and blood"; and "describe the ways in which nutrients and water are transported within animals, including humans".

- **Standards — US (no direct NGSS PE at this band):** NGSS treats the circulatory system as one of the interacting subsystems that transport materials in MS-LS1-3 (middle school); there is no US elementary PE naming heart/vessels/blood. Treat as UK-led and note US placement one band later.

- **Operational details:** Children learn the circulatory system as a TRANSPORT loop: the heart (a muscular double pump) pushes blood through vessels — arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins return it, capillaries are tiny vessels where exchange happens — and blood carries oxygen, nutrients and water to cells and carries waste (like carbon dioxide) away. Key structural facts: the heart has left and right sides; blood makes a round trip (body→heart→lungs to collect oxygen→heart→body). Keep 'double circulation' simple at KS2 (blood passes through the heart twice per loop) — chambers/valves detail and full double-circuit belong to KS3. Connect to the linked Y6 idea that nutrients and water are transported in the blood, and to diet/exercise's effect on the heart.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional). A Y6 child can name heart, blood vessels (artery/vein/capillary) and blood and state their jobs, and describe blood as the body's transport system; the transitional stretch is grasping that blood CIRCULATES in a continuous loop (not a one-way trip that gets 'used up') and that the heart pumps to the lungs AND the body.
bestPractices: Anchor the system in the child's own body: find your pulse, feel the heartbeat, feel it quicken after exercise — so 'the heart pumps blood' is a felt fact before it is a diagram.
Teach it as a continuous LOOP rather than a start-to-end journey, using a closed circuit so children see blood is recirculated and refreshed, not used up.
Name the vessels by DIRECTION (arteries away from the heart, veins back to it, capillaries for exchange) so the labels carry function, not just position.
Keep double circulation simple at KS2 (blood passes through the heart on the way to the body and again after the lungs); defer chambers, valves and the full double circuit to KS3.
Link explicitly to the paired Y6 statement that nutrients and water are transported in the blood, and to diet/exercise effects on the heart, so the strand coheres.
Use colour convention carefully (red = oxygen-rich, blue = oxygen-poor) while flagging the myth that venous blood is literally blue.
keyRepresentations: A closed-loop circulation diagram (heart–lungs–body) with directional arrows and red/blue colouring
A labelled heart showing left/right sides and the connecting great vessels
A vessel comparison (artery thick-walled, vein with valves, capillary one-cell thin) tied to function
An animated blood 'parcel' carrying oxygen/nutrients out and CO2/waste back
A pulse-finding / heart-rate activity linking felt heartbeat to the pumping model
commonMisconceptions: Thinking blood travels one way and gets 'used up', rather than circulating in a continuous refreshed loop.
Believing the heart is on the far left of the chest or is heart-shaped, rather than roughly central and fist-sized.
Assuming blood in veins is actually blue (it is dark red); the blue is only a diagram convention and skin/vein appearance.
Confusing arteries and veins, or thinking arteries always carry oxygen-rich blood (the pulmonary artery does not).
Thinking the heart is a single pump with one path, missing that it sends blood both to the lungs and to the body.

learn.summary: For 10–11 year olds learning the human circulatory system (UK DfE Y6; note NGSS places this at middle school, MS-LS1-3, with no US elementary performance expectation naming heart/vessels/blood). The core objective: name the main parts (heart, arteries, veins, capillaries, blood), describe their functions, and grasp that blood CIRCULATES in a continuous refreshed loop (e.g. body→heart→lungs→heart→body) rather than travelling one way and being 'used up'. Anchor the abstract model to the child's own body (pulse, heartbeat, quickening after exercise), name vessels by direction so labels carry function, and keep double circulation simple (blood passes through the heart on the way to the body and again after the lungs); chambers, valves and the full double circuit are for later (KS3).

activities.title: Drive the circulation loop
feedback: If a learner thinks the blood ends its journey at the body, prompt: trace the blue blood back — which vessels return it to the heart, and where does it go next to collect more oxygen?
When the parcel changes colour at the lungs, highlight: this is the moment the same blood is refreshed and reused, not replaced.
If a learner says arteries always carry oxygen-rich blood, note that the route to the lungs carries oxygen-poor blood away from the heart — direction, not oxygen content, defines an artery.
Point out the red/blue colouring is a diagram convention: oxygen-poor blood is dark red, not literally blue.
activities.rationale: Circulation is a dynamic loop; letting the child drive the pump and watch a parcel complete the circuit, change colour at the lungs, and both deliver and collect materials makes 'blood circulates and is refreshed' concrete. A rest/exercise toggle ties the heart's pumping to the Y6 diet-and-exercise strand. Colour change, vessel labels and a speed toggle are concrete interaction examples, not mandatory mechanisms.
sourceClaims: For KS2: the heart pumps blood around the body; arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry it back, capillaries are tiny vessels; blood transports oxygen, nutrients and water and removes waste such as carbon dioxide.

DfE Y6 statutory requirements: 'identify and name the main parts of the human circulatory system, and describe the functions of the heart, blood vessels and blood'; and 'describe the ways in which nutrients and water are transported within animals, including humans'.
learnerActions: Power a circulation-loop model by repeatedly tapping/pumping the heart so a surge of bright-red (oxygen-rich) blood flows out through the arteries to the body.

Follow a single blood 'parcel': watch it drop off oxygen, nutrients and water and collect carbon dioxide/waste at the body cells, turn blue (oxygen-poor), flow back through the veins to the heart, get pumped to the lungs, release the carbon dioxide and pick up oxygen so it flushes back to red, then start the loop again.
Tap each vessel to label it: arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins return it, capillaries are the tiny vessels where exchange with cells happens.
Toggle a 'rest vs run' control to make the heart beat faster and the flow speed up, then relate this to how your own heart behaves during exercise.
activities.intendedInsight: Blood goes ROUND in a continuous, closed loop and is refreshed at the lungs — it is not consumed on a one-way trip. As it circulates it both delivers (oxygen, nutrients, water) and collects (carbon dioxide, waste). The heart pumps blood both to the lungs and to the body; vessel names describe direction and function.

activities.title: Feel your own pump (pulse and prediction)
feedback: If a learner expects a steady stream, connect the throb they feel to each push of the heart.
If the pulse quickens after exercise, prompt: why would the body move blood faster when muscles are working harder?
Reinforce that any on-screen pump model mirrors their own beating heart.
activities.rationale: Anchoring the model in the child's own body makes the pumping action tangible before it is a diagram, and the predict-then-feel sequence surfaces reasoning. This uses real physical investigation (pulse-finding) as a concrete medium alongside any screen model.
sourceClaims: For KS2: the heart pumps blood around the body; arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry it back, capillaries are tiny vessels; blood transports oxygen, nutrients and water and removes waste such as carbon dioxide.
learnerActions: Find your pulse at the wrist or neck. Before feeling it, predict: does blood leave the heart in a smooth steady stream or in pushes, and why?
Feel the throb with each heartbeat and compare it to your prediction.
Do star jumps or run on the spot, then feel your pulse again and describe what changed.
State in your own words what the heartbeat is doing to the blood and why exercise changes it.
activities.intendedInsight: The heart pumps blood in beats to drive it around the loop; 'the heart pumps blood' becomes a felt fact, and the rate rises with exercise to move more blood (and oxygen) to working muscles.

activities.title: Name the parts and bust the myths
feedback: If a learner says blood only carries oxygen, prompt them to add nutrients, water and the waste (carbon dioxide) it collects.
If a learner confuses arteries and veins, return them to direction: away from the heart = artery, back to the heart = vein.
For the blue-blood myth, clarify oxygen-poor blood is dark red; blue is only how diagrams, and sometimes skin/veins, can appear.
activities.rationale: Naming parts and functions and directly addressing the listed misconceptions consolidates the vocabulary and corrects durable errors. Flap-style 'why does blood keep going round?' and 'what does blood carry?' reveals are concrete interaction examples. A matching/true-false task can check classification but does not by itself elicit extended explanation, so pair it with reasoning in the learner's own words.
sourceClaims: DfE Y6 statutory requirements: 'identify and name the main parts of the human circulatory system, and describe the functions of the heart, blood vessels and blood'; and 'describe the ways in which nutrients and water are transported within animals, including humans'.

For KS2: the heart pumps blood around the body; arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry it back, capillaries are tiny vessels; blood transports oxygen, nutrients and water and removes waste such as carbon dioxide.
learnerActions: Match each part (heart, artery, vein, capillary, blood) to its job.
Explain why blood keeps going round instead of stopping, and list what blood carries (oxygen, nutrients and water delivered to cells; carbon dioxide and other waste carried away from them).
Decide whether this statement is true: 'the blood in your veins is blue' — and explain your answer.

Locate roughly where the heart sits (near the middle of the chest behind the breastbone, tilted slightly to the left, about fist-sized), correcting the idea that it is on the far left or heart-shaped.
activities.intendedInsight: Each vessel's name carries its function; blood is a two-way carrier (delivers and collects); the blue colouring is only a convention, and the heart's real position and size differ from common myths.

activities.title: Order the journey and check understanding
feedback: If a learner says the heart makes new blood, separate 'pump' from 'produce': the heart moves blood; blood cells are made in bone marrow.
If the described path has no return, prompt them to trace blood back through the veins — it's a closed circuit, not an open one.
If capillaries are omitted so the loop has a gap, point out capillaries join arteries to veins and are where oxygen, nutrients and wastes are exchanged with cells.
If only oxygen is named, prompt them to add nutrients, water and the carbon dioxide/waste the blood also carries.
activities.rationale: Sequencing and probing questions assess whether the loop is truly understood and target the specific error patterns (heart makes blood; one-way open path; blood only carries oxygen; missing capillaries). Ordering and selection consolidate but do not by themselves elicit independent construction, so pair them with explanation in the learner's own words.
sourceClaims: For KS2: the heart pumps blood around the body; arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry it back, capillaries are tiny vessels; blood transports oxygen, nutrients and water and removes waste such as carbon dioxide.
learnerActions: Put the blood's route in order: body → heart → lungs (collect oxygen) → heart → body.

Answer: if blood isn't used up, how does the same blood keep delivering oxygen all day? By what route does it get from your toes back to your heart? Besides oxygen, what else is it carrying as it passes your toes? Where does it pick up fresh oxygen?
Choose the correct statement and explain why 'blood only travels one way and gets used up' is wrong.
Describe the heart's job as pumping (not making) blood, noting blood cells are produced in bone marrow.
activities.intendedInsight: The route forms a closed, continuous loop; the heart pumps and does not manufacture blood; capillaries link arteries to veins where exchange happens.

activities.title: Enrichment: explore the heart in three dimensions
feedback: Keep the focus on 'two destinations' rather than full chamber-and-valve anatomy.
If chambers/valves come up, note these are explored in more detail at a later stage (KS3).
activities.rationale: A 3D heart model is optional enrichment that may help visualise left/right sides and vessel connections; at this band the core target remains the transport loop and part functions, so this supplements rather than replaces the loop activity.
learnerActions: Examine a rotatable/cutaway model of the heart to see the left and right sides and how the great vessels connect.
Relate the left/right sides to the idea that the heart pumps blood to the lungs AND to the body.
activities.intendedInsight: The heart is a genuinely three-dimensional muscular double pump with left and right sides feeding two destinations (lungs and body).

constraints: Keep double circulation simple at KS2: blood passes through the heart on the way to the body and again after the lungs. Defer chambers, valves and the full double circuit to KS3.

The target objective is the continuous transport LOOP and part functions; the 3D heart model and any in-role conversation ('talk to a cardiologist') are enrichment/motivational options, not substitutes for driving or tracing the loop.
Red/blue colouring is a diagram convention only — flag explicitly that oxygen-poor (venous) blood is dark red, not literally blue.

Ordering, matching and multiple-choice tasks consolidate and can check vocabulary and route, but recognition-only responses do not by themselves elicit independent explanation; have learners also state the loop and functions in their own words.
Link explicitly to the paired Y6 statement that nutrients and water are transported in the blood, and to diet/exercise effects on the heart, so the strand coheres.
NGSS has no US elementary performance expectation naming heart/vessels/blood; treat as UK-led and note US placement one band later (MS-LS1-3).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the three cited sources (BBC Bitesize; NGSS MS-LS1-3) are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE curriculum claim is marked verified:true. Treat unverified claims accordingly.

The original artefact rationales asserted comparative claims such as 'a static picture cannot' animate circulation and that dialogue 'wouldn't teach the loop as efficiently'. These comparative-efficacy/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements.

Conceptual check: the guidance correctly distinguishes pumping from producing blood (bone marrow makes blood cells) and names vessels by direction (arteries = away from the heart regardless of oxygen content, e.g. the pulmonary artery). No arithmetic, force, fraction or shade-investigation issues arise in this topic.

Fix applied in this review: water added to activity 1's delivered materials (action and insight) to match the cited BBC claim and the DfE 'nutrients and water are transported' statement, which had been dropped from the preferred activity.

assess.poeTask: Have students find the pulse at the wrist or neck and, before feeling it, PREDICT whether blood leaves the heart in a smooth steady stream or in pushes, and why. Feeling the throb with each heartbeat reveals the heart pumping in beats to drive blood around the loop.
probeDeeper: If blood isn't used up, how does the same blood keep delivering oxygen all day?
By what route does blood get from your toes back to your heart?
Besides oxygen, name something else the blood is carrying as it passes your toes.
Where does the blood pick up fresh oxygen before heading out again?
assess.correctAnswer: The blood is not used up. After delivering oxygen it returns to the heart through the veins, is pumped to the lungs to pick up more oxygen, and circulates again in a continuous loop. The heart's job is to pump blood, not to make it — blood cells are produced in bone marrow.

errorPatterns.pattern: The heart makes new blood to replace blood that gets used up
errorPatterns.nextMove: The heart pumps; blood recirculates and is not used up; blood cells are made in bone marrow. Separate 'pump' from 'produce'.
errorPatterns.distractor: The heart makes new blood to replace the blood that gets used up.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the heart produces blood rather than pumping it

errorPatterns.pattern: Blood flows out to the body and is used up — it doesn't come back
errorPatterns.nextMove: Veins return blood to the heart; it's a closed circuit. Trace blood out through arteries and back through veins.
errorPatterns.distractor: The blood is used up delivering oxygen and doesn't return to the heart.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes a one-way, open path with no return to the heart

errorPatterns.nextMove: Blood also carries dissolved nutrients, carbon dioxide and other wastes; it both delivers and collects.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Omits nutrients, carbon dioxide and waste when saying what blood transports

errorPatterns.pattern: Arteries and veins aren't joined — blood somehow jumps between them
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tiny capillaries link arteries to veins and are where oxygen, nutrients and wastes are exchanged with cells.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Leaves out capillaries, so the loop has a gap

responseLevels.gap: Thinks blood is used up and/or made by the heart; no idea of a returning loop.
responseLevels.full: Describes a continuous closed loop — arteries out, capillaries exchanging, veins back, lungs to reoxygenate — with the heart pumping (not making) blood that carries oxygen, nutrients and wastes.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the heart pumps blood carrying oxygen but describes an open path (no return) or omits nutrients/waste and capillaries.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Blood leaves your heart and travels all the way out to your toes. What happens to that blood after it has delivered oxygen to your toes — does it get used up so the heart has to make new blood, or does something else happen? And what is the heart's actual job in all this?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands circulation describes a closed, continuous loop with blood returning and being reused. A child without it thinks blood is consumed and remade, or that the heart manufactures blood.
